Almohad military architecture in Al-Andalus — the tower in its historical context — the Almohad dynasty, which controlled the western Islamic world from Morocco across the Maghreb and into Al-Andalus in the 12th and 13th centuries, built characteristic military structures throughout the Iberian Peninsula — compact, solid, and austere towers and walls that prioritised structural strength over ornament; the Torre de la Calahorra belongs to this tradition; the same Almohad military impulse that built the Giralda tower in Seville (originally an Almohad minaret) and the Torre del Oro produced the walls and towers of Yilliq in the 12th century; Elche's example is smaller in scale but represents the same architectural programme

Not the Córdoba Calahorra — disambiguation essential — the name 'Torre de la Calahorra' is shared by one of Spain's most famous medieval monuments: the Córdoba Calahorra tower at the southern end of the Roman bridge, which guards the approach to the Mezquita from the opposite bank of the Guadalquivir; the Elche Calahorra Tower is an entirely different monument — smaller, less celebrated, architecturally distinct, and located in a different city and region; the two towers share the Arabic name 'calahorra' (al-qal'at al-ḥurra — noble or free fortress), applied to significant fortification points in Andalusi towns, but are not otherwise related; visitors to Elche searching for the Calahorra Tower should not expect the Córdoba bridge tower

description:
The historic centre of Elche is not obvious. The city is surrounded by the most famous date palm grove in Europe — the Palmeral d'Elx, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, 200,000 palm trees planted by the Moors that still shade the city's streets and outlying districts. The medieval town centre itself is compact, its streets narrowed between buildings that have accumulated over eight centuries of continuous occupation since the Christian reconquest. In this historic centre, near the Plaza de la Merced, stands the Torre de la Calahorra: a square limestone tower that is the oldest thing standing in Elche.

The tower dates to the 12th century, the Almohad period. The Almohads — the Berber Muslim dynasty from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco who came to control the western Islamic world and crossed into Al-Andalus to halt the Christian advance — built their military architecture with a characteristic solidity and austerity. Their towers and walls throughout the Iberian Peninsula are recognisable by their compact square plans, their thick limestone or rubble masonry, and their severe absence of decorative elaboration. The Calahorra Tower of Elche belongs to this tradition. It was part of the city walls of Yilliq — the Almohad-era Muslim town that James I of Aragon took in 1265 as part of the progressive Christian reconquest of the Valencian region.

When the reconquest happened and the Christian administration reorganised the city, the Islamic walls were mostly dismantled or absorbed into later construction. The Calahorra Tower survived. Its Almohad masonry was solid enough to outlast the processes of demolition and replacement that consumed most of the Islamic city fabric; its position at a corner of the old wall made it a useful orientation point in the reorganised Christian town. It is the sole surviving fragment of the walls that once enclosed Yilliq. Everything else is gone.

The name 'Calahorra' requires a note. The most famous monument in Spain with this name is the Torre de la Calahorra in Córdoba — the large medieval gateway tower at the south end of the Roman bridge, which today houses a museum of Moorish civilisation and guards the approach to the Mezquita from across the Guadalquivir. That tower is a famous and well-documented monument visited by hundreds of thousands of people each year. The Elche Torre de la Calahorra is a different monument entirely: smaller, less celebrated, and located in a different city on the opposite side of Andalusia. Both share the Arabic name 'calahorra' — derived from al-qal'at al-ḥurra, the noble or free fortress, a term applied to significant military towers in Andalusi towns — but they are not otherwise related. Visitors to Elche should be clear about which Calahorra they are looking for.

The tower is visited as part of the guided walking tour of Elche's historic centre (GYG t894655), which covers both the Calahorra Tower and the adjacent Palacio de Altamira — the late medieval and Renaissance palace that now houses MAHE, the city's archaeological and history museum — in a single circuit. The combination of the two monuments gives a visitor the full temporal span of Elche's surviving built heritage: the 12th-century Almohad tower as the oldest standing structure, and the 14th-century Christian palace that represents the medieval and Renaissance authority that succeeded the Islamic administration. They are within walking distance of each other in the historic centre, and the contrast between them is immediately readable in the architecture — the solid, unadorned Islamic masonry of the tower against the more articulated facade of the later palace.

[Altamira Palace](/castles/spain/altamira-palace) — the 14th-century fortified palace housing MAHE museum, within walking distance in the same historic centre, and covered by the same GYG walking tour. [Santa Bárbara Castle](/castles/spain/santa-barbara-castle) — the great clifftop fortress above Alicante, 15km to the northeast — extends the Alicante province circuit for visitors with more time in the region.
history: 12th century: Torre de la Calahorra built as part of the Almohad-era city walls of Yilliq (Arabic name for Elche); the tower serves as a corner fortification anchoring the defensive perimeter of the Islamic town. 1265: James I of Aragon (the Conqueror) takes Elche as part of the reconquest of the Valencian region; the Islamic city walls of Yilliq are largely dismantled or absorbed into the reorganised Christian town; the Calahorra Tower survives due to the strength of its masonry and its utility as an orientation point in the new urban fabric. 14th–15th century: the Palacio de Altamira established nearby as the seat of Christian noble and administrative power; the Calahorra Tower exists as a relic of the Islamic city within the new Christian urban order. 19th–20th century: historic centre of Elche preserved around the surviving medieval monuments; Calahorra Tower recognised as the oldest standing monument in the city. Present day: tower accessible as part of MAHE circuit and the GYG guided walking tour of Elche's historic centre; sole surviving fragment of the Islamic city walls of Yilliq.
how_to_visit:
**GYG guided walking tour of Elche historic centre (~$59.95/person, t894655, 2–3 hours):** Guided walking tour covering both the Calahorra Tower and the Palacio de Altamira (MAHE) in a single circuit with a licensed local guide. The most reliable way to see the tower with historical context. 0 reviews. Confirm tour schedule before booking.

**Independent visit:** The tower exterior is always visible in the historic centre. Interior access depends on current opening arrangements — confirm before visiting. Elche is approximately 15km from Alicante by road (A-7 motorway, approximately 20 minutes by car) or 20–30 minutes by train from Alicante to Elche Parque station.

**Visiting in context:** The Calahorra Tower is best visited as part of the broader Elche historic centre circuit — Palacio de Altamira / MAHE (within walking distance, 14th-century Christian palace with Lady of Elche replica and Iberian-Roman archaeology), the Basilica of Santa María (17th century, adjacent), and the Palmeral de Elche (UNESCO World Heritage palm grove, a 15-minute walk). Santa Bárbara Castle in Alicante (15km north) extends the province's castle circuit to a full day.

faqs.question: Is this the same Calahorra Tower as in Córdoba?
faqs.answer: No. The Torre de la Calahorra in Elche is a completely different monument from the famous Torre de la Calahorra in Córdoba, which stands at the south end of the Roman bridge and guards the approach to the Mezquita. Both towers share the Arabic name 'calahorra' — derived from al-qal'at al-ḥurra (the noble or free fortress), a term applied to significant military towers in Andalusi towns — but they are architecturally distinct, historically separate, and located in different cities. The Córdoba Calahorra is a late medieval gateway tower with a museum inside; the Elche Calahorra is a 12th-century Almohad defensive tower, the sole surviving fragment of the Islamic city walls of Yilliq. Visitors to Elche should not expect the Córdoba monument.

faqs.question: Why is the Calahorra Tower called Elche's oldest monument?
faqs.answer: The Torre de la Calahorra dates to the 12th century (Almohad period) and is the only surviving element of the Islamic city walls of Yilliq — the Muslim town that preceded the Christian city of Elche established after the reconquest of 1265. Every other standing structure in Elche dates from the Christian period (13th century or later) or has been rebuilt since the reconquest. The Calahorra Tower survived because its Almohad limestone masonry was solid enough to outlast the processes of demolition and replacement that consumed the rest of the Islamic city fabric. Nothing standing in Elche today is older.

faqs.question: Can I visit the Calahorra Tower and the Palacio de Altamira together?
faqs.answer: Yes — both monuments are within walking distance of each other in Elche's historic centre, and the GYG guided walking tour of the historic centre (t894655) covers both in a single circuit. The same tour product is listed on both this page and the Altamira Palace page on this site. The tour places both monuments in the context of Elche's layered historical identity — the 12th-century Almohad tower as the oldest surviving structure, and the 14th-century Christian palace as the seat of the medieval authority that succeeded the Islamic city — making the historical transition between them tangible and readable.
